newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's BCI seeks partner for marriage.
newsitem.headline: Italy's BCI seeks partner for marriage.

text.p: The spotlight is being directed at Italy's Banca Commerciale Italiana: while other big rich northern Italian banks are busy with share issues or merger work, BCI is still searching to find a suitable partner.

Italy's top banks realise they are too small to compete effectively on a European stage. BCI's three northern cousins have been busy at work but BCI, known popularly as Comit, has plenty of money but is still searching how to spend it.

After being rebuffed in two public alliance attempts in the last two years, analysts believe BCI will fall back on its oldest ally, the secretive but powerful merchant bank Mediobanca, and then embark on expansion of its retail banking side.

"A BCI-Mediobanca merger is very likely. BCI would gain from Mediobanca's strong presence on the corporate side and also benefit from Mediobanca's good management," said a Milan banking industry analyst with a London-based investment bank.
"A Mediobanca link would give BCI greater status in the wholesale market, cement their relationship and also that with Generali," said analyst Derek Chambers at HSBC James Capel.

BCI and Mediobanca already have cross shareholdings, with Mediobanca able to sell its products through BCI's retail outlets while BCI and Italy's largest insurer Generali have a joint venture to sell life insurance and pensions in Brazil. Generali is also a close ally of Mediobanca.
"BCI is simply too small, and it has to be a predator as it has around four trillion lire ($2.4 billion) in cash to spend," said a Milan analyst with a British investment banking group.

BCI has seen rival Banco Ambrosiano Veneto beat it in the race to official merger talks with Italy's largest savings bank Cariplo -- a marriage which could create the nation's second largest bank in asset terms.

Another bank Credito Italiano is driving through synergies with Banca Rolo 1473, probably Italy's most profitable bank, where Credito has a 42.2 percent stake after a takeover in 1995 of Credito Romagnolo.
Meanwhile, Italy's biggest bank San Paolo di Torino has just completed a public share offer and is forging closer links with investment bank IMI.

BCI has had a poor history of attempted alliances. After its privatisation in March 1994 it failed in an attempt to buy Ambroveneto in 1995, and earlier this month lost out to Ambroveneto to win the hand of Cariplo.

In April, newspaper reports of a BCI-Mediobanca were hotly denied by both parties, but analysts still say a merger makes a lot of sense. Mediobanca would gain from BCI's retail network to sell more of its products, and BCI would gain from Mediobanca's strong presence on the corporate side.

A combined BCI-Mediobanca could then start to look at Banca di Roma, the last major Italian bank not already linked up in an alliance. Talk of an immediate merger sent Banca di Roma's shares up nearly seven percent last Thursday, after which market speculation has somewhat faded.

However, Banca di Roma is still struggling after the merger of four banks in the early 1990s. Although it is Italy's second largest listed bank in assets it is one of the least profitable suffering from high costs and a poor quality loan book.

But analysts see a possible "Banco di Napoli" action at the Rome-based bank to ring-fence its poor loans into a separate group and make its branch network an attractive proposition for a rich northern bank looking for geographical expansion.

Banco di Napoli recorded the largest ever loss in Italian banking history in 1995, but state-controlled Banca Nazionale del Lavoro (BNL) and former state insurer INA took a 60 percent stake in the bank late last year after the Naples-based bank was stripping out its poor loans.

Some analysts see Banca di Roma as a "potential timebomb" and point out BCI would be better buying a small regional bank to give it strong regional franchises, but others argue it needs to make a big leap forward in its expansion plans. ($1=1,680 lire)
